articles.title: Left-handed university students show higher neuroticism compared to their right-handed peers
articles.summary: A new Austrian study reveals that right-handed students tend to be more extraverted, conscientious, and emotionally stable than left-handers. Researchers also found surprising ways that sex and hand dominance interact to influence depressive symptoms.

articles.title: Remembering a chaotic childhood is linked to psychopathic traits, especially in men
articles.summary: Childhood chaos may shape adult personality more than persistent hardship. A new study in Personality and Individual Differences links an unpredictable early home life to psychopathic traits like meanness and disinhibition, particularly among men.

articles.title: Ayahuasca might protect the brain from stress-induced damage, primate study finds
articles.summary: A new study on marmosets suggests ayahuasca could protect the brain from physical damage caused by chronic stress, pointing to the psychedelic brew's potential as a preventative treatment for depression.

articles.title: Ketamine’s rapid relief of suicidal thoughts may be linked to an increase in morning cortisol
articles.summary: A recent clinical trial found that a single dose of ketamine tends to increase morning cortisol levels in suicidal patients. This surprising hormonal boost persists for 24 hours and may play a role in the drug's rapid antidepressant effects.

articles.title: Machine learning and online tests identify autistic adults with 92% accuracy
articles.summary: Diagnosing autism in adults can be difficult due to long wait times. A new study shows that combining a standard questionnaire with online mental tests and artificial intelligence can predict an autism diagnosis with 92% accuracy.

articles.title: Horror soundtracks can make friendly smiles feel eerie and threatening, study finds
articles.summary: A new study in the Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology suggests scary music subtly alters how people interpret facial expressions. By tracking subjective ratings and eye responses, researchers found ominous soundtracks can make even friendly faces feel threatening.

articles.summary: New research analyzing convicted offenders in South Korea reveals that specific psychological traits vary across different types of within-family murders. Emotional deficits play a pronounced role in distinguishing those who kill their parents from those who kill their siblings.

articles.title: Experts say blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
articles.summary: A new report suggests that blood pressure may be controlled more effectively by increasing potassium while also cutting sodium. Potassium-rich foods can help balance sodium’s effects, but most people consume far less potassium than recommended.

articles.title: AI can tell if your brain is aging faster than you are
articles.summary: A person’s sleeping brain may reveal warning signs of dementia long before memory problems begin. Researchers used machine learning to analyze EEG recordings from about 7,000 adults and found that an older-than-expected “brain age” was tied to a sharply higher dementia risk. Every additional 10 years of brain aging raised that risk by nearly 40%.

articles.title: Scientists discover how obesity may fuel Alzheimer’s disease
articles.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible biological pathway connecting obesity to Alzheimer’s disease. Obesity appears to raise levels of certain fat molecules that can travel to the brain, disrupt its immune defenses, and promote harmful amyloid buildup. Correcting this fat imbalance improved memory and brain function in Alzheimer’s models.

articles.summary: Can a one-year-old's brain structure forecast their childhood intelligence? By analyzing white matter connections using artificial intelligence, researchers discovered that infant brain scaffolding accurately predicts cognitive scores years later, highlighting the early biological foundations of individual ability.

articles.title: What if the brain does not create consciousness?
articles.summary: Christof Koch is taking on one of science’s deepest mysteries: how the brain creates conscious experience, or whether it creates it at all. He argues that materialism has yet to solve this “hard problem” and will explore puzzling phenomena such as near-death experiences and terminal lucidity. His work points toward the possibility that consciousness may be woven into reality itself.
